title: How To Infuriate A Concerned Parent
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Written as a satirical listicle, this piece gives seven deliberately terrible ways to handle a concerned parent — refusing to invite them in, cutting them off before they finish speaking, immediately becoming defensive, blaming their child, refusing to take responsibility, accusing them of raising their voice, and calling them crazy to colleagues. Linsin's central technique is exaggeration: by walking through exactly what defensiveness and ego-protection look like in practice, he illustrates the opposite of what he actually recommends. He explicitly flags step six — accusing a parent of raising their voice — as especially effective at shutting a parent down and discrediting any future complaint they might make. A closing postscript makes the satirical intent explicit, stating plainly that he isn't recommending teachers anger parents and that the article is a literary device meant to make a sharper point than a straightforward list of dos and don'ts would. He points readers toward the site's Handling Parents archive and his book Unstressed for the genuine, non-satirical guidance.

quotes: The biggest mistake you can make is to hear them out. The more they can provide proof of their concerns, the more dangerous it is for you.
You never want to do this. Protect your ego at all costs. Besides, you always know better.
This strategy is the chef’s kiss. It will shut them down and burn their insides out.
If you see even a hint of yourself in any of the seven steps, I want you to know that parents aren’t your enemy and there are honest guidelines you can follow.
To be clear, of course I’m not recommending that you anger parents. The article is a literary device intended to make a strong point.
